group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
An 86-year-old man was transferred by wheelchair from the skilled-nursing wing of a long-term care facility after staff noted two days of progressively deeper cough that turned purulent overnight and was now interspersed with brief, sharp stabs of right-sided pleuritic discomfort; he had refused the facility’s standing order for acetaminophen so that “the hospital can see the real numbers,” and the nurse escorted him in a private van without supplemental oxygen, nebulized therapy, intravenous fluids, or antibiotics. His chart from the home lists hypertension controlled with amlodipine 5 mg daily and remote adenocarcinoma of the sigmoid colon resected six years ago followed by adjuvant capecitabine, with no evidence of recurrence on surveillance CT performed five months earlier; there is no documentation of chronic kidney impairment, cirrhosis, or heart muscle dysfunction, and his most recent metabolic panel three weeks ago showed a creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL. He quit a 20-pack-year cigarette habit three decades ago, drinks only tea, and has never used illicit substances. Immunization records at the facility confirm both pneumococcal series and this season’s inactivated influenza vaccine. Upon stretcher arrival he sat upright, breathing through pursed lips and clutching his right flank with each cough; mucous membranes looked dry, skin was hot and flushed, and capillary refill was under two seconds. Untreated triage vitals on ambient air at this sea-level institution were: oral temperature 102.6 °F, irregularly regular radial pulse 137 beats per minute confirmed on telemetry as atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, automated right-arm blood pressure 148/76 mm Hg corroborated by manual measurement, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute with mild supraclavicular retraction, and pulse oximetry 94 % on room air. Neck veins were not distended, and no peripheral edema was appreciated. Cardiac auscultation revealed a fast S1 and S2 with variable intensity, no murmurs or extra sounds. Pulmonary examination demonstrated absent breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the lower half of the right posterior thorax with egophony superiorly; scattered coarse crackles peppered the remaining fields, left greater than right. The abdomen was soft, nondistended, and nontender, with a well-healed midline laparotomy scar. A finger-stick glucose obtained before vascular access read 146 mg/dL. Venous chemistry drawn within ten minutes—before any saline flush—returned sodium 168 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L, chloride 112 mEq/L, bicarbonate 26 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 64 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. Complete blood count showed leukocytes 18.9 × 10⁹/L with 89 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 58 %, hemoglobin 19.1 g/dL, and platelets 220 × 10⁹/L. A right radial arterial sample on room air demonstrated pH 7.71, PaCO₂ 23 mm Hg, PaO₂ 102 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 29 mEq/L, consistent with marked respiratory alkalosis with mild hypoxemia. Serum lactate was 2.0 mmol/L, high-sensitivity troponin fell below assay detection limits, and NT-proBNP was 190 pg/mL (similar to a value on file from his last outpatient visit). A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph obtained fifteen minutes after arrival—prior to any therapeutic intervention—revealed dense consolidation occupying the right middle and lower lobes accompanied by a concave superior meniscus that obliterated the right costophrenic angle, compatible with a free-flowing effusion; the cardiac silhouette was within normal limits for age, mediastinal contours were unchanged from prior imaging, and lung volumes were slightly reduced. Point-of-care thoracic ultrasound confirmed an anechoic layer measuring approximately 2.5 cm in depth posteriorly and demonstrated dynamic air bronchograms in the adjacent parenchyma. Twelve-lead electrocardiography showed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response at 136 bpm, nonspecific ST-T wave changes, and no acute ischemic pattern when compared to a tracing from the nursing facility two months prior. Two peripheral sets of blood cultures, an induced sputum specimen for Gram stain and culture, urinary Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella antigens, and a multiplex viral PCR panel were sent before empiric antimicrobials or other agents were ordered. As this note is entered he remains seated upright on 21 % inspired oxygen, has not yet received intravenous crystalloid, bronchodilators, antipyretics, diuretics, corticosteroids, or parenteral antibiotics, thereby preserving all vital signs, laboratory results, and imaging findings above as his untreated presentation physiology.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
Apply the Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) to the untreated presentation:
- Demographics: male age 86 → 86; nursing-home residence → +10.
- Examination: RR 36/min (≥30) → +20; pulse 137/min (≥125) → +10. No altered mental status, SBP 148 mmHg (not <90), and temperature 39.2°C (neither <35 nor ≥40) → 0 each.
- Tests: BUN 64 mg/dL (≥30) → +20; pleural effusion → +10. Arterial pH 7.71 (not <7.35), sodium 168 (not <130), glucose 146 (not ≥250), hematocrit 58% (not <30%), and PaO₂ 102 (not <60) → 0 each.
- Comorbidities: no documented liver disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, or renal disease → 0 each. The neoplastic-disease item is worth 30 points, but standard PSI criteria count cancer active at presentation or diagnosed within the past year. The colon cancer was resected six years ago without evidence of recurrence.
The standard sum is 86 + 10 + 20 + 10 + 20 + 10 = 156. Counting the remote cancer history instead gives 156 + 30 = 186; this result depends on that nonstandard inclusion.
Final answer: 186
